title: A Jesuit pope
hook: Francis brought discernment into the language of the whole Church

segments.voice: Yesterday, men and women for others, Arrupe's hard question to proud former students. Your line was for others. When you looked back, who was the day really for? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.

Discernment can sound like a word that belongs in retreat houses and novitiates: quiet rooms, a spiritual director, someone deciding whether to become a priest or a sister. Then a Jesuit from Buenos Aires, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, became Pope Francis. And the word came with him. It turned up in his letters to the whole Church, in his talks to young people, in what he said to married couples, in the way he asked bishops to meet and listen. A retreat-house word went out into kitchens and parish halls. Today, the pope who brought it.
screen: `A RETREAT-HOUSE WORD.` → `A JESUIT BECOMES POPE.` → `THE WORD GOES TO THE KITCHENS.`

segments.voice: A Jesuit pope. Francis had made the Spiritual Exercises, had given them to others, and had been a novice master and a Jesuit provincial in Argentina. So when he wrote, the Ignatian vocabulary came along. In his letter on holiness, Rejoice and Be Glad, he gives the closing pages of a chapter to discernment. He says it isn't only for rare, dramatic decisions. It's for daily life: small choices, ordinary days. He recommends something that will sound familiar from this path: a sincere daily examination of conscience, looking back over the day with God. And he insists it's a gift to ask for, not a technique to master, and that it means listening: to God, to others, to reality, and especially to the poor. Saint Paul gives the old instruction in the Douay-Rheims: "But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Prove means test, try out. Francis was asking every Catholic to do that, not only people in retreat houses. He also brought the word into how the Church makes decisions, asking for meetings where people would pray, speak freely, listen, and then discern together, rather than simply vote. The word went with him into those rooms. Here is why it matters day to day. Discernment isn't the same as deciding. Deciding asks what do I want. Discernment asks, in the quiet, which of these good options draws me toward God and others, and which pulls me inward and away? It's this week's whole Jesuit vocabulary, handed to everyone.
screen: `A POPE FORMED BY THE EXERCISES.` · `DISCERNMENT FOR ORDINARY DAYS.` · `A GIFT TO ASK FOR, AND LISTENING.` · `DECIDING VS. DISCERNING.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: discern one choice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a real, small decision in front of you: whether to say yes to an invitation, how to spend an evening, what to say in a hard conversation. Hold the first option for a few breaths and notice what moves in you: peace, restlessness, energy, dread. Then hold the second the same way. Don't decide yet. Just notice which one draws you outward, toward God and others, and which pulls you inward. If you pray, you can ask for light. The bell holds the time.
A Jesuit pope. Pope Francis, formed by the Spiritual Exercises, who carried the language of discernment from retreat houses into the life of the whole Church. Today's word.
Your line: discern. Today, before one small choice, pause and ask not just what do I want, but which way draws me toward love. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-nine.
